results.title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
results.content:
As AI systems become more capable, they are increasingly able to produce long and difficult
mathematical proofs, including solutions to long-standing open problems
(OpenAI, 2026; Alman and Williams, 2026).
At the same time, it is becoming harder to verify
the correctness of these proofs. Existing verifiers, including outcome and process reward models,
were built for problems with a short checkable final answer (Lightman et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Rahman et al., 2025), whereas a proof has no final answer to check; its
correctness lies in whether every step follows from the ones before it. Formal verification in a
proof assistant such as Lean offers an alternative, but translating an informal proof into a formal [...] LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench.
Because LeanPRM requires no human annotation, it can scale with the capabilities of frontier provers, turning progress in proof generation into stronger verifier models. [...] We make three contributions.

LeanPRM, to our knowledge the first framework that uses Lean to produce step-level correctness
labels for natural-language proofs at scale, and its corpus of 10,634 labeled proofs
(Section 2).

LeanPRM-Bench, a held-out benchmark of 200 natural-language proofs with step labels, which we
release for evaluating proof verifiers (Section 2.2).

A controlled evaluation showing that, with the same recipe and training budget, verifiers
trained on LeanPRM outperform verifiers trained on existing human-labeled verification data
on four of five
benchmarks, select better proofs at test time on IMO-level problems, and improve at every model size
from 0.6B to 8B on three of the five benchmarks (Section 3).

results.content:
### Developer Practical Guide & Quickstart

Reasoning teams can explore the `LeanPRM` dataset, models, and `LeanPRM-Bench` evaluation suite at ` to plug automated step-level verifiers into Best-of-$N$ or RL post-training pipelines. Pretraining engineers designing memory-efficient sliding-window architectures can attach `CPLM`'s lightweight copy-paste head to retain full-context token copying fidelity at ~3% compute overhead.

⚔️ Launch VS Compare→💳 View Plans↗

Up NextProgressCompass: Context-Aware Embodied Progress Reward Models Drive Long-Horizon Agent Planning

Read Now→ [...] Copy-Paste Language Models (`CPLMs`): Augments the standard LM head with a lightweight Copy-Paste (CP) head (~3% compute overhead) that creates an alternative gradient path bypassing the vocabulary projection bottleneck. When paired with sliding-window attention (SWA), the CP head enables direct token retrieval across the full context without requiring expensive interleaved full-attention layers. [...] LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Step Supervision Without Human Labels: A generator LLM produces a natural-language proof paired step-by-step with a formal Lean 4 proof without interactive Lean feedback. The Lean compiler checks every step, and a secondary filter discards failures caused solely by formal syntax so that negative labels pinpoint genuine mathematical errors. This automated pipeline yields 10,634 proofs with 152,000 step-level labels and zero human annotation.

results.title: GitHub - pavelslab-nyu/LeanPRM: Code for LeanPRM · GitHub
results.content:
```
python prepare_data.py --dataset pavelslab-nyu/LeanPRM --historical-validation --output data/paper python train.py --data-dir data/paper --model Qwen/Qwen3-4B --output runs/leanprm-4b --dry-run
```

Remove `--dry-run` to train. The launcher uses the paper's 300-update GRPO configuration. `verifier_task.py` contains the prompt and reward. Omit `--historical-validation` to use the final validation split. LeanPRM-Bench is the dataset’s test split. The dataset card explains historical validation overlap.

`solver_task.py` prepares the solver baseline and supplies its reward. `convert_prm800k.py` prepares the PRM800K baseline. Pass separately prepared solver data to `train.py --task solver`. [...] Remove `--dry-run` to generate. Use `--model` and `--review-model` to select available models. Current generation preserves the initial natural-language steps during review. Some historical runs allowed natural-language cleanup, so the published corpus is the reference for reproducing the paper.

`pipeline/select_numina.py` and `pipeline/select_balanced_hf_statements.py` select source statements. `pipeline/classify_difficulty.py` provides the difficulty classifier. `pipeline/filter_corpus.py` filters generated proofs and supports excluding held-out theorem groups.
